podcast.title: Founding (1966)
podcast.body: Sire Records was established in New York City in 1966 by Seymour Stein and Richard Gutterher with an initial investment of ten thousand dollars. "1966, two guys, Seymour Stein and Richard Gutterher. They took ten thousand dollars and they set up a record label in New York City that they called Sire Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: First Domestic Signing (The Ramones - 1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Seymour Stein discovered the Ramones in a Manhattan bar and signed them, making them one of Sire's first domestic signings. This was significant as other labels had rejected the Ramones for being too unconventional. "But then in 1975, Seymour decided to check out a bar in one of the scusiest parts of Manhattan and this is where he found the Ramones and they became one of Sire's first domestic signings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Marketing New Wave (1976)
podcast.body: Facing radio resistance to "punk rock," Sire Records, under Seymour Stein, initiated a marketing campaign around Christmas 1976 urging the use of "New Wave" to describe their new signings, like the Ramones. This strategy successfully removed the punk stigma and propelled the term into mainstream acceptance. "So Sire launched a NAD campaign called Don't Call It Punk, urging people to call this new music New Wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: First "New Wave" Compilation (1977)
podcast.body: Sire Records (referred to as "Fono Grande de Estados Unidos") released what is noted as almost the first compilation album titled "New Wave" in 1977. This album was a "catch-all" that included a diverse mix of artists such as Ramones, Talking Heads, and The Residents, highlighting the early, diffuse nature of the New Wave movement. "la discográfica de la Fono Grande de Estados Unidos en el 77 se acabó un recopilatorio llamado New Wave casi el primer recopilatorio que se llama New Wave, y que es un cajón de sáster donde está todo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Pioneering "New Wave" Marketing (Early 1977)
podcast.body: Sire Records invented the term "New Wave" as a marketing strategy in early 1977, launching a campaign called "Don't Call it Punk." This aimed to re-brand British punk rock into a more palatable and commercially viable genre for the North American market, fostering new opportunities for bands like The Pretenders, Depeche Mode, Elvis Costello, Echo & the Bunnymen, The Cure, and The Smiths. "And before the company was bought by Warner and ceased to be an indie label, someone in the office invented a new term."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Acquisition by Warner Brothers (1978)
podcast.body: Sire Records was acquired by Warner Brothers in 1978, at which point it ceased to be an independent label and became part of a major label operation. "But when Sire was acquired by Warner Brothers in 1978, they became part of a major label operation."

"Seymour Stein, the owner of Sire Records, a label which was having success with groups like The Ramones, Talking Head and The Pretenders, was inspired by the Ramones covering Needles and Pins to sound the searches to a two album deal."

podcast.title: Decision to Withhold "Into the Groove" (1985)
podcast.body: After the "Vision Quest" dispute, Sire Records made the decision not to issue "Into the Groove" as a single in America, fearing it would divert radio attention from other Madonna releases. Instead, it was placed on the B-side of a 12-inch single, making it eligible only for Billboard's Dance Charts. "In the US, Sire put into the groove on the B-side of a 12-inch single, making it eligible for Billboard's Dance Charts, but not the Hot 100."

podcast.title: "Don't Call It Punk" Campaign
podcast.body: Recognizing that punk carried too much negative baggage in North America, Sire Records launched a marketing campaign for its new signings under the banner "Don't Call It Punk." They consciously rebranded these acts as "New Wave" to make them more acceptable to American audiences. "Sire launched a marketing campaign for these new signings under the banner, don't call it punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "New Wave" as a Marketing Solution
podcast.body: During a marketing meeting, a suggestion was made to use the term "new wave" instead of "punk" to describe Sire Records' new signings. This strategic rebranding proved successful in "wiping away" the stigmas and suspicions attached to punk, thereby allowing bands like Talking Heads and Blondie to gain radio play and public acceptance. "And so it came to pass that at a marketing meeting at Sire Records, someone suggested that they use the term new wave in place of punk to describe their new signings. And it worked, just like that."

podcast.title: Champion of New Music
podcast.body: Seymour Stein and Sire Records were pivotal in supporting new music, particularly post-punk and new wave, in North America. Stein loved the new sound and signed bands like The Ramones, The Dead Boys, and The Talking Heads. "Which is where we meet Seymour Stein and his people at Sire Records."

podcast.title: Championing Early Punk
podcast.body: Sire Records was one of the few labels interested in the Ramones when other companies ignored them. The band chose Sire because they felt the label "understood us best" and would not get "lost in the shuffle." Sire booked the Ramones into a studio for their debut album, which cost $6,400 to record. "Sire had the Ramones booked into a recording studio at Radio City Music Hall on February 2nd, 1976."

podcast.title: Commercial Failure of Searchers Albums
podcast.body: Despite critical success, The Searchers' albums for Sire Records did not perform commercially, leading the label to drop them. "Unfortunately, while those albums had some critical success, they did nothing commercially, and Sire dropped them."

podcast.title: Founder Seymour Stein's Impact
podcast.body: Seymour Stein, the founder of Sire Records, is highly regarded for signing a diverse and influential roster of artists, including iconic acts like The Ramones, Talking Heads, and Madonna. His label later released an album by The Mighty Lemon Drops, a band that originated from the NME's influential *C86* compilation, showcasing Stein's significant role in the development of indie and alt-rock. "It's originally from a 1998 album entitled The Boy with the Arab Strap and the song is about Seymour Stein, the founder of Sire Records and the guy who signed everyone from the Ramones to the Talking Heds to Madonna."

podcast.body: Sire Records was an independent New York record label founded by Seymour Stein. It became instrumental in the New Wave movement, notably being among the first labels to sign influential bands like The Ramones and The Talking Heads. podcast.body: The original plan for Sire Records was to distribute British and European records in the United States, which they successfully did for a period. "And their plan was to simply distribute cool British and European records in the United States."

podcast.title: Key Signings and Imports
podcast.body: Seymour Stein, as founder of Sire Records, was responsible for signing seminal acts like The Ramones and The Talking Heads. He also gave Madonna her "first proper record deal" and imported "unknown English bands" such as The Smiths, The Pretenders, and The English Beat into the North American market. "He's the guy who signed the Ramones and the Talking Heds. He's the guy who gave Madonna her first proper record deal. He's the guy that imported unknown English bands like The Smiths and The Pretenders and The English Beat into North America."

podcast.title: Marketing Crisis (New York City)
podcast.body: Sire Records, based in New York City, encountered a marketing crisis because mainstream radio stations refused to play their new punk rock signings, such as The Ramones, due to the genre's controversial and perceived dangerous nature. "A record label called Sire was having a marketing crisis. The head of the company, a guy named Seymour Stein, was a fan of what was happening at CBGB and had signed a bunch of these new bands, including the Ramones."

podcast.title: North American Distributor for The Smiths
podcast.body: Sire Records was responsible for distributing The Smiths' music in North America, playing an important role in the band's reach beyond the UK. "The Smiths, with this charming man released on Rough Trade in the UK and distributed North America by Sire Records, a very important part of our history of indie music."

podcast.title: Pioneering "New Wave" Marketing
podcast.body: To circumvent American radio stations' reluctance to play "punk" records—which were seen as weird, violent, or a mere fad—Seymour Stein, founder of Sire Records, ingeniously began marketing his artists under the term "New Wave." This strategy aimed to "disguise things and soften the blow," making the music more acceptable for mainstream radio play and thereby commercially launching the New Wave genre. "That's when Seymour started using the phrase New Wave to market his stuff. It was a way to disguise things and soften the blow."
